analysis.one_liner: Extended Medicare-style health coverage to all U.S. residents and added long-term care benefits, financed by new taxes.
analysis.headline: Introduced with a single cosponsor, the universal health and long-term care bill never received a committee markup or vote and died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.
analysis.plain_summary: The Mediplan Act would have put every U.S. resident into a public health plan with Medicare-equivalent benefits, with no cost-sharing for children, pregnant women, and people below the poverty line, and a $2,500 annual out-of-pocket cap for everyone else. It would have expanded Medicare nursing home coverage and created a new long-term care benefit covering nursing homes and home-based care for chronically ill seniors. The program would have been financed by new income taxes on individuals, a tax on corporations and other entities, and a payroll tax on employers' wages.
analysis.who_benefits: Every U.S. resident would gain Medicare-equivalent coverage with automatic enrollment at birth. Children under 23, pregnant women, and people below the poverty line would pay no deductibles, coinsurance, or copays, and would get benefits Medicare does not cover: outpatient prescription drugs, eyeglasses, hearing aids, well-child care, and unlimited inpatient hospital stays. All other beneficiaries would get a $2,500 annual out-of-pocket cap, and no doctor or hospital could bill patients beyond the government rate. Medicare skilled nursing coverage would expand from 100 to 180 days a year with no prior hospital stay required, and chronically ill people 65 and older would gain coverage for nursing home care and home and community-based care, with no cost-sharing for those below 200% of the poverty line.
analysis.who_benefits_short: All residents, especially children, pregnant women, and low-income people

how_it_helps.text: Makes every U.S. resident eligible for a Mediplan plan with the same benefits as Medicare Parts A and B, enrolls people automatically at birth, and issues Mediplan cards for claims.

Eliminates all deductibles, coinsurance, and copays for children under 23, pregnant women, and people below the federal poverty line, and adds prescription drugs, eyeglasses, hearing aids, well-child visits, prenatal and postnatal care, and inpatient hospital care without time limits for these groups.

Caps every beneficiary's annual out-of-pocket costs for deductibles, coinsurance, and copays at $2,500, replacing Medicare's separate hospital and medical deductibles with a single $500 deductible, and bars providers from billing patients above the government payment rate.
Expands Medicare skilled nursing coverage from 100 to 180 days per year, removes the requirement that it follow a hospital stay, and extends home health services to up to 180 consecutive days.

Creates a new long-term care entitlement covering nursing facility services and long-term home and community-based care for chronically ill people (age 65 and older until 1997), with case-management assessments, written care plans, appeal rights, no cost-sharing below 200% of poverty, and payment based on a prospective system rather than provider costs.

Finances the program through a dedicated Mediplan Trust Fund fed by new income taxes, a tax on all non-individual taxpayers, an employer payroll tax, and the Medicaid savings states must pay into the fund.

analysis.who_pays: Individuals would pay a new additional income tax; corporations and every other non-individual taxpayer would pay a new tax; and employers would pay a new tax on the wages they pay. States would have to send their Medicaid savings (their 1990 low-income medical spending, indexed to inflation) to the Mediplan Trust Fund each year as a condition of their residents remaining eligible. Providers would take Medicare-level payments with no extra billing allowed, and drug makers would be paid under a new prospective payment system.
analysis.who_pays_short: Individuals, corporations, and employers, through new taxes

drawbacks.text: The program would be financed by broad new taxes: an additional income tax on individuals, a tax on every non-individual taxpayer including corporations, and a payroll tax on employers' wages, with no tax-cutting offset anywhere in the bill.

Working-age adults who are not low-income would still face a $500 deductible and up to $2,500 in annual out-of-pocket costs, and the core benefit package is Medicare-equivalent, so outpatient drugs, eyeglasses, and hearing aids would be covered only for children and low-income people.

The long-term care benefit is phased in slowly and narrowly: until 1997 only people 65 and older qualify, and for services in 1993 and 1994 a person must have already spent at least 12 of the prior 24 months in a nursing facility before benefits are payable, leaving younger disabled people and most new patients without help for years.

A state's residents lose Mediplan eligibility unless the state keeps paying its 1990 Medicaid level, indexed to inflation, into the federal trust fund, which locks in state health spending regardless of need.

The bill enforces insurers' obligation to keep supplemental benefits for people already enrolled in group plans through a private lawsuit with triple damages, inviting litigation against employers and plans.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core bargain was large and real: Medicare-level coverage for everyone, first-dollar coverage for children, pregnant women, and the poor, and a nursing home and home care benefit that did not exist anywhere in federal law, paid for by taxes spread across individuals, corporations, and employers. The design was cautious rather than sweeping: it kept substantial cost-sharing for working adults, kept Medicare's existing payment systems and private claims processors, paid home care less than nursing home care, and delayed long-term care for anyone under 65 until 1997, so the early years would have delivered less than the headline promise. The bigger weakness was political: with one cosponsor and no committee action, none of these tradeoffs was ever debated or voted on.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to two House committees, which routed it to their health subcommittees, and no one ever held a markup or vote before the Congress ended in January 1991.

narrative.text: Rep. Pete Stark introduced the Mediplan Act on July 18, 1990, with Rep. William Coyne as the only cosponsor; it was referred jointly to the Ways and Means and Energy and Commerce Committees.
Within three weeks the bill had been sent to the Ways and Means Health Subcommittee (July 27, 1990) and the Energy and Commerce Health and Environment Subcommittee (August 3, 1990).
Neither committee took any further action: no hearings, no markup, no vote are recorded, and the bill died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Private health insurers and employers came out ahead: no public plan displaced private coverage, and no new income, corporate, or payroll taxes were ever levied. People without adequate coverage, and families facing nursing home costs, gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Private insurers, employers, and taxpayers who would have paid

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill's entire recorded support was two House Democrats (1 of 257 in the caucus cosponsoring), and no Republican signed on, so the partisan shape was never tested.

industries.note: Mediplan would pay Medicare rates for a benefit package replacing most private coverage; insurers could sell supplemental benefits only to people already enrolled in group plans on enactment day. Their Medicare-style claims-processing role as carriers and intermediaries would have continued, but their core insurance business would largely disappear.

Employers would pay a new tax on wages, but group health plans would only have to maintain supplemental benefits for people already enrolled, allowing them to stop buying core health coverage for their workforce.

The new long-term care title would create a federal payer for nursing facility care with prospective payment adjusted for case mix and wages, opening a revenue stream for care now paid out-of-pocket or through Medicaid, though payment would be set prospectively rather than at cost.

industries.industry: Home care, homemaker, and adult day care agencies
industries.note: Long-term home and community-based care, including homemaker services and adult day care, would become a covered entitlement paid at 70% to 90% of nursing facility rates, greatly expanding a market served mostly by unpaid family caregivers today.

Doctors would gain a universal payer at Medicare rates, but only on an assignment basis with no balance billing, obstetric care paid as a global fee, and caesarean payments set 5% lower to discourage surgical delivery.

The bill extends Medicare's section 1876 HMO rules to Mediplan from the start and directs a report on adapting HMO provisions to long-term care, keeping HMOs as paid delivery channels for the new universal program.
